title: How to Build Custom Payment Routing Rules
summary: Learn how to build custom payment routing rules by payment method, issuer, geography or cost, and set up safe failover for eligible transactions.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


### TL;DR


- Custom payment routing rules choose an eligible gateway, processor, or acquiring bank using details such as the payment method, issuer, amount, or country.
- Set a priority for overlapping rules and a default route for transactions that match none.
- Use failover for eligible failures once you have checked the original payment status. Track success rates, processing costs, and fallback frequency after launch.


When customers make payments online, they expect transactions to be processed quickly, securely, and without interruptions. The right payment route can vary by payment method, issuing bank, transaction amount, location, or provider.


Custom routing rules allow businesses to define how payment transactions should be directed to different payment gateways, payment processors, or acquiring banks based on specific conditions. Businesses can use these rules to choose among eligible routes for each transaction.


A well-designed payment routing system can help businesses improve[payment success rates](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-payment-success-rate/) , manage transaction costs, and reduce avoidable checkout failures.


##


What Are Custom Routing Rules in Payment Integration?


Custom routing rules are predefined conditions that determine which payment gateway, payment processor, or acquiring bank should handle a particular transaction.


In a payment integration setup, businesses may connect with multiple[payment service providers (PSPs)](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-service-provider/) ,[payment gateways](https://www.cashfree.com/payment-gateway-india/) , or acquiring banks. Each provider may have different processing capabilities, transaction costs, supported payment methods, and approval rates.


Custom routing rules help businesses decide which provider should process a transaction based on predefined parameters.


For example, an online business may have integrated three payment gateways. It can configure these routes.


- Routes UPI transactions through Gateway A.
- Routes domestic credit card transactions through Gateway B.
- Routes international card transactions through Gateway C.
- Sends eligible transactions to an alternative gateway if the primary gateway is unavailable.


##


How Custom Payment Routing Rules Work


Custom routing rules work through a decision-making mechanism within the payment infrastructure. When a customer initiates a payment, the payment system evaluates the transaction details against predefined conditions and selects the appropriate payment route.


### Step 1. The Customer Starts a Payment


The customer visits a website or app, adds products to the cart, and proceeds to checkout. They select a payment method, such as UPI, credit card, debit card, or net banking.


### Step 2. The System Collects Routing Inputs


The payment integration system receives the relevant transaction information. Available fields depend on the integration.


- Transaction amount
- [Payment method](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-mode-types/)
- Card network (Visa, Mastercard, RuPay, etc.)
- Issuing bank
- Customer’s country or payment instrument country, where available
- Transaction currency
- Merchant account details


### Step 3. The Engine Evaluates the Routing Rules


The routing engine checks the transaction details against the configured rules. For example, if a business has created a rule to route international card payments through a particular payment processor, the system identifies transactions that meet this condition.


### Step 4. The Engine Selects a Payment Provider


Once a matching rule is identified, the transaction is directed to the selected payment gateway, processor, or acquiring bank for authorisation.


### Step 5. The Provider Returns a Payment Status


The selected provider processes the transaction and returns a response, such as successful, pending, declined, or failed due to a technical issue. Use the provider’s[payment lifecycle](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/online/resources/payment-lifecycle) to determine which statuses are final.


### Step 6. The Engine Applies Eligible Failover


If the selected provider experiences a technical issue or becomes unavailable, the system may route the transaction through an alternative provider, provided the failure is eligible for retry and the original attempt has a confirmed outcome.


This process can happen in the background. Depending on the payment method and provider, the customer may need to authenticate again or select another method.


##


8 Types of Custom Payment Routing Rules


Businesses can create different routing rules depending on their payment requirements, customer base, transaction volume, and payment infrastructure.


Here are some common types of routing rules used in payment integration.


### 1. Payment Method-Based Routing


Payment method-based routing directs transactions to specific payment providers depending on the payment method selected by the customer.


For example, a business could assign each payment method to a different provider.


- Route UPI transactions through Provider A.
- Route credit card transactions through Provider B.
- Route debit card transactions through Provider C.
- Route net banking transactions through Provider D.


This approach is useful when different payment providers offer better processing capabilities or performance for specific payment methods.


### 2. Bank-Based Routing


Bank-based routing directs transactions based on the customer’s issuing bank or the bank involved in processing the payment.


For example, a business may configure a routing rule to send transactions from customers using HDFC Bank cards through one acquiring bank and transactions using ICICI Bank cards through another.


This can help businesses work with providers that have better processing performance for particular issuing banks.


However, the availability of bank-level routing depends on the payment method, processor integrations, and transaction information available to the routing engine.


### 3. Transaction Amount-Based Routing


Transaction amount-based routing directs payments to different providers based on the transaction value. Businesses can define different routes for low-value and high-value payments.


A business could use these transaction bands.


- Transactions below ₹5,000 are routed through Provider A.
- Transactions from ₹5,000 to ₹25,000 inclusive are routed through Provider B.
- Transactions above ₹25,000 are routed through Provider C.


This approach can help businesses manage processing costs, transaction limits, and provider-specific requirements.


### 4. Geography-Based Routing


Geography-based routing directs transactions based on the customer’s country, region, or the location associated with the payment instrument.


For example, an Indian e-commerce business selling internationally may use these routes where its acquiring arrangements permit them.


- Domestic card payments through an Indian acquiring partner.
- US-issued card payments through a US acquiring partner.
- European card payments through a European acquiring partner.


Using an appropriate local acquiring route can help businesses improve payment acceptance and manage[cross-border processing requirements](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/global-payment-apis-crossborder-collections-and-payouts/) . A card’s country alone cannot establish a merchant’s eligibility for local acquiring.


The exact benefits depend on the provider, issuing bank, currency, and applicable regulations.


### 5. Card Network-Based Routing


Card network-based routing directs card transactions based on the network associated with the customer’s card. For example, a business may configure different payment routes for:


- Visa
- Mastercard
- RuPay
- American Express


If one acquiring partner offers better processing performance for a particular card network, the business can prioritise that partner for the relevant transactions.


### 6. Cost-Based Routing


Cost-based routing directs transactions through payment providers based on their processing fees.


Different payment processors may charge different fees depending on the payment method, card type, transaction location, and business arrangement.


For example, if Provider A charges a lower processing fee for a particular card category than Provider B, the business may prioritise Provider A for those transactions.


This helps businesses manage payment processing expenses while considering approval rates and transaction reliability.


### 7. Success Rate-Based Routing


Success rate-based routing selects payment providers based on their historical or real-time transaction performance. For example, if Provider A has a higher success rate for[UPI transactions](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/upi-transaction-limit/) than Provider B, the routing engine may prioritise Provider A for UPI payments.


The system can evaluate several performance signals.


- Transaction approval rates
- Technical failure rates
- Provider response times
- Bank availability
- Payment method performance


Performance-based routing can adjust decisions as transaction conditions change. Compare approval rates for similar transactions so one provider’s mix of issuers or payment methods does not skew the result.


### 8. Failover-Based Routing


Failover routing automatically redirects eligible transactions to an alternative payment provider when the primary provider encounters a technical issue.


For example, a customer initiates a UPI payment through Provider A. However, Provider A experiences a temporary technical issue and cannot process the request. The routing system identifies the issue and attempts to process the transaction through Provider B, if it confirms the first attempt did not succeed and the retry conditions permit it.


Failover routing helps businesses maintain payment continuity and reduce disruptions caused by provider downtime.


Retry decisions should depend on the failure reason and the certainty of the original transaction status. A technical timeout can leave a payment pending. Check for[late authorisation](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/late-payment-authorisation/) before sending another attempt. Follow provider and network rules for declines such as insufficient funds, an incorrect UPI PIN, or a customer-imposed limit. For cards, check the applicable[network rules for resubmitting a decline](https://cis.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/download/about-visa/visa-rules-public.pdf) .


##


How to Set Up Custom Payment Routing Rules


1. **Map eligible providers.** List the payment methods, currencies, countries, and transaction limits each provider supports. Check your acquiring agreements before activating a route.
2. **Set rule priority and a default route.** Evaluate specific rules before broader ones. For example, an eligible international card above ₹25,000 might match both a country rule and an amount rule. Decide which takes priority and what happens when neither matches.
3. **Test retries and duplicate handling.** Use test transactions to cover success, declines, timeouts, and delayed responses. Track each attempt against the same order and use verified[payment webhooks](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/webhooks) and provider status checks before retrying a payment or fulfilling the order. Make repeated requests safe to process by using idempotency keys where the provider supports them.
4. **Roll out gradually and measure.** Start with a limited share of eligible payments. Compare first-attempt and overall success rates, processing cost per successful payment, and fallback frequency. Check how the new route affects[payment reconciliation](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/ecommerce-payment-reconciliation/) before expanding it.


##


Conclusion


Building custom routing rules is an important step towards creating a flexible and reliable payment integration system. It gives businesses greater control over how transactions are processed across different payment providers, payment methods, banks, and geographical regions.


By defining appropriate routing conditions, setting rule priorities, configuring fallback mechanisms, and monitoring provider performance, businesses can improve payment reliability and manage processing costs more effectively.


As transaction volumes grow and businesses expand into new markets, custom routing rules can help create a payment infrastructure that is easier to manage, optimise, and scale.


##


Frequently Asked Questions


#### What is a custom routing rule in payment integration?


A custom routing rule is a predefined condition that determines which payment gateway, processor, or acquiring bank should handle a transaction. It uses parameters such as payment method, transaction amount, card network, issuing bank, or customer location to select an appropriate payment route.


#### Do businesses need multiple payment gateways to create routing rules?


Some payment providers offer routing across multiple acquiring banks or processing partners through a single integration. Businesses building their own multi-provider routing infrastructure generally need multiple connected payment processors or gateways.


#### Can custom routing rules reduce payment failures?


Yes. They can reduce technical payment failures by directing transactions towards providers with better availability and processing performance. Insufficient balance, incorrect UPI PINs, and exceeded transaction limits require a different response from a provider outage.


#### What is the difference between payment routing and payment orchestration?


Payment routing determines which provider processes a transaction based on predefined conditions or performance signals. Payment orchestration is a broader infrastructure that manages multiple payment providers, routing decisions, retries, failover, and transaction monitoring.


#### What happens when a payment gateway becomes unavailable?


If a payment gateway becomes unavailable, a configured failover rule can redirect eligible transactions to an alternative provider. Before retrying, the system should verify the original transaction status to prevent duplicate charges.


#### How can businesses monitor custom routing rule performance?


Businesses can monitor routing performance through transaction success rates, technical failure rates, provider response times, processing costs, and fallback frequency. Reviewing these metrics helps identify underperforming routes and optimise routing conditions. Compare the same payment method and issuer across providers.
